Newsletter edition

Draft · proposal for BBE

Subject (2 options)
  1. Seven sites, and not one trip
  2. If you only have time for one Atlantic Forest site recommended
Preheader (2 options)
  1. Ten of our guides ranked where the birding is best. Our advice for one visit is short. recommended
  2. The ranking is the easy part. Here is what it means for your trip.

Seven sites. Not one trip.

We asked ten of our guides where the birding is best in Brazil's Atlantic Forest. It is ten professional opinions, not a count of species. Caio Brito wrote up the results.

The seven, in the guides' order

  1. Intervales, São Paulo
  2. Itatiaia, Rio de Janeiro and Minas Gerais
  3. Serra Bonita, Bahia
  4. Urupema, Santa Catarina (tied)
  5. Ubatuba, São Paulo (tied)
  6. Campos do Jordão, São Paulo
  7. Boa Nova, Bahia

What the ranking does not tell you The post's first caveat is that these seven places do not add up to one trip. The biome is big and varied. What is left is somewhere between 11 and 16 percent of the original forest, most of it in small fragments (Ribeiro et al., 2009, as the post cites it).

If you can only see one Intervales. It is the only site all ten guides named. Our advice: give it three full days.

Read the post The scoring, how we handled ties and what each place offers: Read "The 7 Best Birding Sites in Brazil's Atlantic Forest"

At BBE, birding is not a race for species. It is an observation-first practice led by biologists. A long checklist is a natural result of birding this way.

If you have more time The post sketches a route through several of these places and says it is more or less the shape of our Southeast/South Brazil Supreme Tour. The tour runs from 17 November to 14 December 2027, groups of up to 8. List price on the tour page: USD 11,700; single supplement extra. See the tour

— Brazil Birding Experts

How to read this calendar

This is a sample for a portfolio. It is not BBE's calendar and does not state BBE's posting frequency, active channels or measurement.

How to read it

  • Period: four weeks, month to be chosen (December 2026 or January 2027). There is no audience data to prefer one month. Weeks are numbered 1 to 4, without dates. No tour departure is used as an anchor.
  • Audience: international birding travelers reading in English (working hypothesis, to be confirmed with BBE).
  • Channels: Instagram, Facebook, YouTube, newsletter, blog.
  • Next step for the audience: in each item, move the reader from the channel to the long-form content (post, video or page). Call to action and offer: to be defined with BBE.
  • Indicator (set before publishing): clicks through to the long-form content, read from each channel's native dashboard (Instagram and Facebook: Meta Business Suite; YouTube: YouTube Studio; newsletter: email platform; blog: GA4 and Search Console). Window: 7 days per item. No target and no benchmark; values left empty.
  • Slots are examples, not frequency. The grid shows what fits in four weeks in a portfolio. It does not say what BBE publishes or what an ideal rhythm would be. No days, no times, no "ideal" number of posts.
  • Pilot before batch: the week 4 Reel depends on the week 2 Reel pilot being reviewed at full size.
  • Editorial themes are labels for what BBE has published on its blog and YouTube (trip reports, species, "Meet" videos, conservation, method). They are not approved editorial themes.
  • Any video quote or timestamp is to be checked against the audio before use.

Outside the grid

  • Blog (EN): no new post in the calendar. The blog is the destination of the links (the posts cited above). Public observation, not a BBE plan: between 30 Mar and 30 Oct 2026 the blog has 9 dated posts, with gaps from 10 days to about 6.5 weeks.
  • Second newsletter edition: not included (only if the first is accepted).

Summary

  • Items: 9 (Instagram 6, Facebook 1, YouTube 1, newsletter 1; blog as link destination).
  • Themes: trip reports (1.2, 3.1), method (1.1, 2.1), "Meet" series (Caio 2.2, Tati 2.3, Ciro 4.1), species and conservation (3.2, 4.2).

Not included

Frequency, days, times, hashtags, "ideal" number of posts, goals, follower counts, reach, any performance value.

Description (EN): first two lines

Tati Pongiluppi is a biologist, co-founder of Brazil Birding Experts (BBE) and the person who runs the company behind the scenes.
In this video she tells how birds took her from a university lab to almost ten years at SAVE Brasil, a motorcycle expedition, and BBE.

Description (EN): body

As a child in the Atlantic Forest of São Paulo, Tati says, her parents showed her the birds in the backyard. The video follows her from a university lab and a 2004 ornithology congress, through SAVE Brasil, to joining Ciro Albano and Caio Brito as BBE was starting. She also tells how her role moved from guiding trips to the work behind the scenes, which shows in the trips but is rarely seen.

Ciro Albano is part of her story: they met at an event, became friends, and he invited her to work with him. In his own biography video, Ciro calls Tati the pillar of BBE's structure (from the English subtitles of that video): https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0rqpZo5KHyI

1b · Long-form content

↑ Back to contents

How to Choose a Birding Tour in Brazil: Five Questions to Ask Before You Pay

Draft · proposal for BBE

A tour page can promise a long list of birds. It cannot tell you who will stand beside you on a narrow trail at dawn, how many of you there will be, or what happens when it rains for three days.

Advice pages on choosing a birding tour tend to return to the same few themes: the leader, the size of the group, the pace and the real price. Travellers often ask about the same things. This article takes those questions one at a time. For each, it explains what to ask, what one Brazilian operator says about its own practice, and what you can check for yourself.

That operator is Brazil Birding Experts (BBE), a company of biologists and ornithologists that leads birding tours across Brazil. Everything BBE says about itself here is attributed to BBE, because a company's description of its own practice is a claim, not proof. Where possible, the article points to something outside the sales page: a guide's public profile, a published trip report, the tour's own terms. The strongest example is a 19-day trip report from 2025, which this article uses as a case throughout.

1. Who is leading the tour?

Ask for the name of the lead guide, not the title. Then ask what training and track record that person has, and whether that same person will lead your departure.

BBE says that every lead guide is a biologist, that several hold master's degrees or PhDs, and that many have published papers and books on the birds and regions their guests visit. Its tour policy draws a line between "counting a bird and understanding it."

Here is how you can check. BBE publishes a page for each team member it lists. Caio Brito's, for example, lists an M.Sc. in Zoology from the Federal University of Paraíba and links to his public profiles on eBird, iNaturalist, xeno-canto and WikiAves. The tour page for the Rondônia/Acre Popular departure of June 2027 names him as the guide.

A public profile shows what a guide has recorded and shared. It does not show how that guide treats eight people at 5:40 a.m. For that, you need a second kind of evidence: a trip report written by the guide, with dates, misses and decisions in it. Section 4 uses one.

2. How many people will be in the group?

Ask for the maximum group size, not the typical one. Ask whether that number includes the guides. And ask what the operator does so that everyone gets a turn at the front of the trail and the best seat in the vehicle.

BBE's tour pages reviewed for this article list a maximum group size of 8, and 6 on its Amazon tours, including Rondônia/Acre. Its reason, in its own words: crowding a trail harms the habitat and the experience, "and because a smaller group simply sees more." It also says that everyone takes turns at the front of the line, and that seats in the vehicle rotate.

The 2025 report shows what group size means in practice. On day 2, the guide describes a Sooty Antbird (Hafferia fortis) appearing on a narrow trail that was "too tight for eight people," so some saw it and others did not. That group was six participants and two guides.

A small group is not a guarantee, either. On day 6, the report says a calling Alta Floresta Antpitta (Hylopezus whittakeri) was seen by part of the group, not all of it. The honest question is not "will everyone see every bird?" It is "what do you do when someone does not?"

3. What is the pace, and who sets it?

Ask for a typical day by the clock. Ask how far you will walk, when you rest, who can change the plan and on what grounds.

BBE says that on most days breakfast is at 5:00 to 5:30 a.m. and the group leaves right after. It says the rhythm is "set by the birding rather than by covering distance," while warning that on some Amazon tours you will walk at a brisk pace for a few kilometres to reach the sites of certain target species. (A target species is a bird a group has set out to find on a given day.) For Rondônia/Acre, the tour page rates the difficulty "medium": seven kilometres or more a day on uneven forest trails, in heat above 35 °C, with built-in rest days. Its FAQ adds that the pace is often brisk.

On safety, BBE says its guides have "full authority to adjust, delay or stop a plan."

The report shows these rules under pressure:

  • Plans change. On day 2, when the main target did not appear where expected, the guide changed plans and drove to the places where he had heard or seen it before. On day 5, hearing that another group had found the Rondônia Bushbird (Clytoctantes atrogularis) that morning, the guides went for it the same afternoon, because seeing it early "changes the whole spirit of the trip."
  • Logistics bend the schedule. On day 13, a vehicle tire had a bulge and fuel was low. Lunch ran late, the afternoon start slipped to 4:30 p.m. and the guide wrote that "safety came first."
  • Fitness matters. On day 17, the group walked more than 13 kilometres on muddy slopes. The guide adds that the temperature never went above 24 °C, and that "under typical Amazon heat it would have been a very different story."

Notice what these notes give you. They are not a promise of an easy trip. They are a record of how decisions were made when things went wrong.

4. What does the species list actually mean?

Ask three things. Are the species on the tour checklist ones that participants saw, or ones the guide heard? What share of that checklist do groups usually see? And which birds does the operator treat as the priority?

BBE answers all three in its FAQ. The numbers it quotes are species seen by participants on previous editions, not species heard only by the guide. The tour checklist covers all records for the areas visited, and since not every habitat is visited, "it is very rare to see everything on it." In BBE's words: "we usually see about 80% of the list. Our priority is to see all the Brazilian endemics that occur along the route, not the length of the list." (An endemic is a species found only in Brazil.) It also says that a long checklist is a natural result of this way of birding, but that the experience comes first.

The Rondônia/Acre report shows what a trip list looks like from inside. Its final notes say the group covered 3,172 km by car, plus a couple of hundred by boat, and recorded 555 bird species, 63 of them heard only. The report does not say how many were seen by everyone. It links 50 separate eBird checklists, one or more per session, which you can open and read. That count was made from the page; it is not a BBE statistic.

The report also records its misses. The Buff-cheeked Tody-Flycatcher (Poecilotriccus senex) was tried for on four days without success before it finally showed on day 14. The Red-and-black Grosbeak (Periporphyrus erythromelas) had not appeared by day 12; the guide adds, "don't feel special if you did not see it."

The report ends with a poll. Each of the six participants and the two guides chose their six favourite birds; the guide scored them from 6 points for a first choice down to 1. The winner, with 23 points, was the Rufous Potoo (Nyctibius bracteatus), a bird that came straight in to a speaker placed behind the rooms of a lodge at night. The Rondônia Bushbird, which the report names near the top as one of the route's emblematic species, scored 9. Eight voters on one trip prove nothing general. But the poll shows what a checklist cannot: what a group remembered.

Ask any operator for a trip report or eBird checklists from a past departure. BBE says elsewhere that every tour adds records to eBird and GBIF. Its FAQ says guides go through the day's list with the group every evening, and that "some guides also keep eBird checklists for the tour and share them with you." So ask whether the checklists of your departure will be shared with you.

One more test is a question: which month, route or fitness level would the operator advise against? BBE's guide to the best months for birding grades each month, and for its lowest grade it writes: "if you can choose, we would rather send you somewhere else in Brazil in that month." Its Terms of Use add that it "cannot guarantee any specific sighting." A clear answer to that question tells you more than a promise.

5. What does the price actually cover?

Ask what the price is for: per person, in what kind of room, for how many days. Then ask for the "included" and "not included" lists of the specific tour, not of the company in general. They differ from tour to tour.

Take one BBE departure as an example. The Rondônia/Acre Popular tour of 2 to 20 June 2027 is 19 days long. The tour page, read on 21 November 2026, shows a list price of USD 10,700 and a single supplement of USD 1,100, listed separately. Its FAQ states: "Prices are per person in a double or twin room." The page lists as included: accommodation in double rooms, all meals with one beverage each, all transportation, tour leader and local guides, entrance fees, and drinking water and snacks. It lists as not included: additional drinks, "any flights not mentioned above," and personal items such as laundry.

BBE also publishes its payment and cancellation terms. According to the tour page FAQ and its Terms of Use, a confirmation deposit of 25% secures a place (35% on Pantanal tours), and the balance is due 90 days before departure. A traveller who cancels is not refunded but receives credit toward a future tour, valid for two years: the deposit becomes credit if you cancel 120 days or more before departure, and the credit falls to 60% and then 40% of the tour price as the date nears. Flight tickets already issued are not credited. The Terms strongly recommend travel insurance. BBE's home-page FAQ, as recorded for this article, lists tips and insurance among the things not included, along with international flights.

Read all of this before you pay, and ask which flights are inside the price. One thing this article cannot say for BBE or any operator is what financial protection exists if the company fails, because it has no source. Ask for that in writing.

If a species is essential to you, say so before booking. BBE says it will give "a realistic answer," and that if a trip is not a good fit for your fitness or health, it will tell you before you book.

Five questions to put to any operator, including BBE

  1. The guide. Who exactly will lead my departure? What have they published, recorded or taught, and where can I see it?
  2. The group. What is the maximum size? Does it include guides? How do you rotate trail positions and seats?
  3. The pace. What does a typical day look like by the clock? How far do we walk, and when do we rest? Who can change the plan, and when? Which month or fitness level would you advise against?
  4. The list. Are the species numbers on the tour checklist seen or heard? What share do groups usually see? Can I read a trip report or eBird checklists from a past departure?
  5. The price. For what, per whom, and in what room? Which flights, tips, drinks and insurance are inside, and which are outside? What are the payment, cancellation and financial-protection terms, in writing?

An operator that answers these five plainly, with something you can check, is telling you how the trip will actually run. A long list of species is only the result.

[to be defined with BBE: CTA]

Artigo curto (PT)

Rascunho · proposta para a BBE

Written in Portuguese. Portuguese layer and the “nós” voice are a labelled hypothesis: the BBE site and blog have no Portuguese version today.

Perto de casa, com calma: o que pesa numa saída para observar aves

Quando alguém pergunta onde começar a observar aves na Mata Atlântica, a resposta mais útil não começa por um lugar. Começa pela forma de observar. Escolher entre Intervales e Itatiaia importa menos do que saber como você quer passar o dia na trilha.

Este texto é para quem observa aves no Brasil e está planejando uma saída perto de casa. Em vez de uma lista de lugares, contamos aquilo de que cuidamos nos nossos roteiros e que vale para qualquer saída. Para a lista de lugares, há o post que Caio Brito, biólogo e cofundador da BBE, escreveu em 30 de outubro de 2026, em inglês.

Com quem você vai

Todo guia-líder [termo a validar] da BBE é biólogo. Para nós, a diferença está em observar com alguém que estuda essas aves, conhece a ecologia delas e lê a floresta, e não com quem só quer completar uma lista.

Perto de casa, isso vira uma pergunta simples: quem conhece este lugar? Em Intervales, por exemplo, o post de Caio diz que a maior parte do parque exige guia local.

Nossos guias cuidam das pessoas tão de perto quanto cuidam das aves. Eles gostam de dividir o que sabem, e perguntas são sempre bem-vindas.

Quantas pessoas vão

Mantemos os grupos pequenos, sempre dentro da capacidade de suporte de cada lugar, porque aglomerar uma trilha prejudica tanto o hábitat quanto a experiência, e porque um grupo menor simplesmente vê mais.

O que se decide antes de entrar

Alguns lugares têm mais de um modo de visitar. Itatiaia, o primeiro parque nacional do país, criado em 1937, tem uma parte baixa, de mata, e outra de altitude, e cada uma tem as suas aves. Segundo o post, a parte baixa se entra pela cidade de Itatiaia e a alta, por Itamonte. Escolha a parte antes de sair de casa.

O ritmo

O ritmo de um dia de observação é dado pela observação, e não pela distância percorrida. Eficiência em campo, para nós, não é correr: é experiência, preparação e capacidade de se adaptar às condições. Por isso os guias cooperam em rede e contam com dicas recentes e um plano A, B e C para cada dia. Guias locais, donos de pousada e pesquisadores nos mantêm atualizados sobre lugares, estações e avistamentos recentes.

O clima faz parte disso. O post de Caio lembra que Intervales pede roupa de chuva de novembro a abril, e que Intervales e Ubatuba ficam mais fáceis de maio a setembro.

O que se faz com a ave

Playback, para nós, é uma ferramenta que tem um preço a pagar. Usamos sequências curtas, em volume baixo, dirigidas a uma espécie específica, com o guia observando como a ave reage e parando assim que a pergunta é respondida. O silêncio também é uma resposta. E nunca espantamos uma ave para ter uma foto melhor ou uma vista mais clara: o bem-estar dela vem antes da observação.

Por que fazemos assim

Caio Brito conta, em vídeo do nosso canal, qual é o objetivo: "O nosso maior objetivo [é] encantar através das aves do Brasil."

Para ir além

A página "How We Bird" explica o método em detalhe, em inglês: How We Bird. O detalhe de cada lugar está no post de Caio: The 7 Best Birding Sites in Brazil's Atlantic Forest, Ranked by the Guides Who Work There.

[a definir com a BBE: CTA/oferta]

Na BBE, observar aves não é uma corrida por espécies. É uma prática de observação em primeiro lugar, conduzida por biólogos. Uma lista longa é resultado natural de observar assim, mas a experiência vem primeiro.

Traduções do inglês: nossas. Amostra de portfólio, não uma publicação da BBE.

Fontes conferidas; mapa de afirmações disponível. A definir com a BBE: canal onde o texto sairia; CTA/oferta; áudio do trecho de Caio (12:23) conferido por humano.

Is a BBE trip for you?

Brazil Birding Experts · biologists and ornithologists who lead birding tours across Brazil

1. Will I get up early? Yes. On most days breakfast is at 5:00 to 5:30 am. The pace is set by the birding, not by the distance we cover.

2. Will the group wait while I photograph? We are not a photography tour: the group does not wait for photographs once everyone has seen the bird well.

3. Will I be one of many? No. Groups are up to eight (six on our Amazon tours), always within each site's carrying capacity, because crowding a trail harms both the habitat and the experience, and because a smaller group simply sees more.

Want a trip built around you? Tell us your dream, we design your route, we handle everything, you bird and we guide. Private groups of one to eight.

Write to us. Write to us before you book, with what you hope to see. [to be defined with BBE: contact, QR code and CTA]

7 · Measurement

↑ Back to contents

Channel tracking dashboard

Draft · proposal for BBE

This is a sample for a portfolio. It is not BBE's dashboard and does not state that BBE measures any channel today. All value fields are empty on purpose: the dashboard defines what to read, from where and how, before any number exists.

The dashboard measures what the pieces ask of the reader (read, save, write), not how many follow BBE. Each window ends in one decision: keep, adjust or stop a piece or a format. Who decides, and by what criterion, is to be defined with BBE before the first window. No target and no goal.

Dashboard

How to read each column. Window value stays empty until someone with account access fills it in, with date and window. Dated public observation is what anyone can see on the profile on 20 Nov 2026: it is not an internal metric, not performance, has no goal or target, and is not part of the reading rule.

It does not prove that the named channel caused the trip (observed, not incremental).[empty][no public observation]

General rules

  1. No target, goal, benchmark, "best time" or ideal frequency in this version. Whoever sets a goal decides and records it with the source.
  2. Each value enters with channel, source, reading date and window; without all four, the field stays empty.
  3. Follower and review counts are observation, not the result of a piece; they are not part of any reading rule.
  4. Observed vs. incremental: without a test with comparison, the dashboard describes what happened, not what the piece caused.
  5. BBE (or whoever has access) chooses what to track; this dashboard is a proposal for the portfolio.

Notes on the visual identity

This page follows the direction of BBE’s own website: full-width photography, Lora headlines in blue, Roboto text, rounded cards with a teal tag, pill buttons, and sections that alternate white, cream and teal.

The look follows BBE’s own identity: blue #304A96, cream #F5F2E5, dark teal #006D74 for small text, Lora for headlines and Roboto for text. The logo is the site file, used only on light backgrounds and at 120 px or wider.

BBE currently places its blue-macaw logo on the dark green of some Instagram slides, where it is hard to see. Here the logo appears only on cream or white. suggestion
